paragraphs.text: Dystonia-25 is an autosomal dominant form of primary torsion dystonia. In the families reported by Fuchs et al. (2013), onset was usually in adulthood and most often in the neck. The dystonia stayed focal in some patients and spread to segmental or generalized dystonia in others. Cranial and speech involvement were common, but arm involvement was less frequent.

paragraphs.text: Bressman et al. (1994) examined 53 individuals from 4 generations of a non-Jewish North American family with adult-onset idiopathic torsion dystonia. Seven family members were affected, with a mean age at onset of 28.4 years (range, 7 to 50 years). In 6 of the 7, the neck was affected first. All 7 developed cervical dystonia, and 5 had dysarthria or dysphonia.

paragraphs.text: Fuchs et al. (2013) reported 28 mutation carriers with definite dystonia from 8 families. Mean age at onset was 31.3 years (range, 7 to 54 years). Onset was in the neck in 82% of patients, and 93% had neck involvement at their last examination, but only 46% still had focal dystonia. Cranial involvement was seen in 57% and speech involvement in 44%. No patient had onset in the arms, and only 32% developed arm involvement. The authors noted that this feature distinguished GNAL dystonia from DYT6.

paragraphs.text: Fuchs et al. (2013) performed exome sequencing in 2 families with primary torsion dystonia and identified heterozygous mutations in the GNAL gene. Family P carried a nonsense mutation (S293X) and family D1 carried a missense mutation (V137M). In family D1, V137M was among the 20 missense variants shared by all 4 sequenced members, and it segregated with the disease. Sanger sequencing of 39 additional multiplex primary torsion dystonia families that were negative for DYT1 and DYT6 identified GNAL mutations in 6 more families (19%). These were a missense mutation (E155K), 2 frameshift insertions (S95fsX110 and R198fsX210), a possible splice site mutation (c.274-5T-C), a nonsense mutation (R21X), and an in-frame deletion (P102-V104del). None of the variants were present in dbSNP135, about 3,500 European exomes, or 572 control chromosomes. Segregation analysis confirmed that the mutations were transmitted with the disease in all families for which DNA from multiple affected individuals was available.
